activity: tone differences, public versus private spaces and common conventions of online communication
knowledge_domain: tone differences, public versus private spaces and common conventions of online communication
fact: One of the first written guides to online manners, 'Netiquette Guidelines', was published in 1995 as a document called RFC 1855.
story:
The morning the class group chat fell apart, Nicholas was eating a granola bar in the computer lab and watching Mr. Fortin's face turn a slow shade of purple. Somebody, and nobody would admit who, had sent fourteen messages in a row the night before, all in capital letters, ending with a cartoon explosion. Half the class had replied with more capital letters. Two kids had typed arguments in ALL CAPS so long that the chat looked like one enormous shouting wall.

"Enough," Mr. Fortin said. "New rule. Before this chat continues, we're going to write proper rules for it. Nicholas, you like puzzles. Figure out if anyone has ever actually written official manners for the internet. Margaret, Lexa, help him. Report back tomorrow."

Nicholas presumed somebody must have, because every game he'd ever played came with a rulebook, and the internet was basically the biggest game ever invented. At lunch he and Margaret sat hunched over the library computer while Lexa spun a chair in lazy circles, announcing that she was growing lethargic from research and needed snacks. The smell of floor wax and old paper made the whole thing feel like a detective movie.

"There has to be something," Margaret muttered, typing words like "official internet manners" and "rules for talking online." Then Nicholas noticed something odd in the results, the way a fisherman notices one ripple in a flat lake. Several pages mentioned a document with a strange code name. He clicked, and there it was, plain as a lunch menu.

"Listen to this," he said. "It's called RFC 1855."

"Sounds like a droid," Lexa said, abandoning her spinning.

"It's real, and it's from 1995." Nicholas skimmed the page. "One of the first written guides to online manners. The actual title is 'Netiquette Guidelines.'"

Margaret wrote it all down in her careful looping handwriting, and then they read on, because now they were curious how much had changed. The old guide said things like not typing everything in capital letters because it looked like shouting, and thinking before you sent a message to a whole group when it was really meant for one person. "Wait," Lexa said, sitting up straight for the first time all lunch. "People were worrying about this before my parents even met?"

"That's the best part," Nicholas said. "The problem isn't new. Only the chat is new."

The next day they stood in front of the class with a poster Margaret had made, with the code name in giant letters across the top. Nicholas explained that the shouting caps had a history, that people had been working on this exact annoyance for decades, and that the class could borrow from the old rules instead of inventing everything from scratch. He felt a small burst of pride, the kind that comes from finding a hidden pattern rather than winning a prize. Nobody, he realized, had a monopoly on good manners, but somebody had written them down first, and that somebody deserved a thank-you.

The class voted on three rules: no caps, no message floods, and private arguments sent privately. Mr. Fortin added the poster to the wall beside the whiteboard, where it hung slightly crooked.

"Somebody should tell the capitol-letters kid," Lexa whispered, "that people saw him coming in 1995."

Nicholas straightened the poster, stepped back, and said, "Better than that. Now he can look it up himself."

activity: saying goodbye to a grandparent who has died
knowledge_domain: saying goodbye to a grandparent who has died
fact: In Judaism, shiva, from the Hebrew word for 'seven', is a seven-day period of mourning after a burial, when visitors come to comfort the family.
story:
Nathaniel stood at the edge of the hospital bed where his grandfather lay, his hands still smelling of the hand sanitizer by the door. The machines had been turned off an hour ago, and the room felt strangely large without their beeping. His mother had gone to fill out papers at the desk, so it was just him and the quiet and the thin winter light through the blinds. He touched his grandfather's hand once, cold and still, and said the only thing he could think of. "I'll see you at the house, Zayde. Everybody's coming."

Everybody did come. After the burial, his mother set up low chairs in the living room and covered the mirror with a sheet, and for the rest of that first day neighbors filed through with casseroles. On the second morning, the doorbell rang and Jayke stood on the mat, holding a card so folded and refolded it had gone soft. Quentin was behind him, balancing a box of the chocolate cookies Zayde always kept in his cupboard. "I didn't know what to write," Jayke said, staring at his shoes. "I started like eight times. Every verdict I came up with sounded wrong."

Nathaniel had been wondering about that too, in a quiet way. People kept arriving, sitting, saying almost nothing, and leaving. At first he had thought they were waiting for his mother to start something, some speech or ceremony, but no speech ever came. He tested his idea out loud. "I don't think you're supposed to say the right thing. I think you're just supposed to be here." He pointed at the low chairs and the sheet over the mirror. "It's called shiva. Seven days. That's what the word means." Quentin looked around at the full couch, the plates of food, the aunt who was already refilling the kettle, and nodded slowly, like he was checking the math.

They sat for an hour. Jayke never did read his card, but he listened to Nathaniel's uncle tell a story about Zayde's rebellious youth, how he had once skipped his own graduation to see a baseball game, and Jayke laughed at the right part and then looked guilty about laughing, and Nathaniel's mother said, "Laughing is allowed. He'd want that." Quentin methodically allocated the cookies onto three plates, one for each of them, and pushed the box toward the middle of the table where anyone else could reach it.

When the boys stood to go, Jayke finally handed over the card, unopened. "You don't have to read it now," he said. "Just, whenever." Nathaniel put it in his pocket, and his mother walked them to the door and thanked them for coming, twice, because once didn't seem like enough. At the threshold Jayke paused. "Day five," he said. "We'll be back on day five."

activity: to test whether a solution is an acid or a base using litmus paper and the pH scale
knowledge_domain: to test whether a solution is an acid or a base using litmus paper and the pH scale
fact: Lemon juice has a pH of about 2, which makes it strongly acidic compared with most things people drink.
story:
Ms. Asante set a tray of unlabeled cups on the lab bench and said whoever identified the mystery liquid correctly would earn the last bonus point of the term. Aiden eyed the cups the way other kids eyed a pop quiz. He wanted that point, mostly because Franklin had beaten him on every other one.

The paper strips came next. "Litmus," Ms. Asante said, holding one up. "Dip, wait, read. Red means acid. Blue means base. Neutral changes nothing." She did not say which cup was which, and she did not say that the pH chart on the wall was there to be used, but Aiden noticed that the numbers ran from zero to fourteen, with seven sitting in the middle like a fence.

Franklin picked up the cup on the far left and sniffed it. "It's lemon juice. That's easy. Lemon juice is food, and food is neutral, so it's a seven." He looked extremely satisfied with this chain of reasoning. Layne, who was frugal with words, said only, "Test it."

Aiden dipped a strip into his own cup first. Nothing. Not a flicker of red, not a hint of blue. "Mine's the neutral one," he said, and wrote seven on his worksheet. Then he dipped a fresh strip into Franklin's lemon juice. The paper turned red so fast it was almost rude. But Aiden had learned something from the chart: red only told him acid, not how much acid. There was a second kind of strip in the box, one that changed through a range of colors, and he laid it against the pH chart until the shades matched.

"Two," he said. "It's a pH of about two." Franklin's expression suggested he had been personally betrayed by a fruit. Layne leaned over and checked the chart. "Seven's neutral. Two is way on the acid side. Strongly acidic." Franklin said, "Compared with most things people drink, that seems dramatic." Aiden pointed out that a controversy over a lemon was not going to earn anyone a bonus point.

They worked through the rest of the cups, extracting answers one strip at a time, and Franklin got the baking soda solution wrong by calling it vinegar. Ms. Asante walked the rows, pausing at Aiden's worksheet. She picked it up, read the two beside the lemon juice, and set it down again.

"Someone," she said, "did not assume." She moved on before Franklin could argue that assuming had simply been faster. Aiden folded his worksheet in half, the way people fold things they intend to keep.

activity: the idea of a hypothesis as a testable guess that an experiment can support or overturn
knowledge_domain: the idea of a hypothesis as a testable guess that an experiment can support or overturn
fact: The independent variable is the one thing an experimenter changes on purpose to see what happens.
story:
Scarlett knelt in the community garden between the bean trellises and the compost bins, staring at the limp seedlings in bed four. In bed two, the same beans stood tall and green. Same seeds, same watering can, same week of planting. "So there's something different about this bed," she said to Henri, who was crouched beside her poking at the soil. "Something we can't see."

"Like what?" Henri asked.

"That's the thing. I have a guess. My guess is that the soil in bed four is bad, maybe because somebody dumped something in it. A guess you can test, that's called a hypothesis. You set up something and see if it proves you wrong or not." She pulled a trowel from her bag. "So here's my test. We plant beans in fresh store soil and in bed four soil, side by side in pots, same water, same sun. If the bed four soil ones fail, my hypothesis stands. If they all grow fine, I was wrong about the soil."

They filled six pots from Mr. Haile's supply shed, three with bagged soil and three scooped from the mysterious bed. On the way out, Mr. Haile handed Scarlett a folded note, since he was heading out and couldn't stay. "Found this taped to the shed door," he said. "Thought it was yours."

Back at Scarlett's porch, she opened it. "To whoever keeps the garden," the message read, "I modified the watering schedule in bed four this week. Also added new mulch. Hope that's all right. Your ambassador from the Thursday volunteers." Scarlett read it aloud twice. "They changed two things."

Henri frowned. "Is that bad?"

"Think about it. If the beans perk up now, we won't know if it was the water or the mulch. We'd believe my soil idea was wrong, but maybe the water alone was the problem and the soil is fine." She tapped the note against her knee. "When you test something, you're only supposed to change one thing on purpose. Mr. Haile calls that the independent variable in his class, I think. It's the one thing an experimenter changes on purpose to see what happens."

They set the six pots along the porch rail and agreed on a rule: every pot got the same amount of water at the same hour, so their results would be consistent and nothing extra could sneak in. Each morning before school, Scarlett measured the seedlings with a ruler and wrote the numbers in her notebook. By Friday, the fresh-soil beans had stretched nine centimetres. The bed four beans sat at four, pale and sulking.

"Your hypothesis," Henri said slowly, reading over her shoulder. "It's holding up."

"It's not proven yet," Scarlett said, but she was already writing a reply to the Thursday volunteer and tucking it into the shed door: "Please change only the water next week, nothing else, so we can figure out what's really going on in bed four." She pressed the tape down flat with her thumb and looked back toward the porch, where three pale pots waited in a row.

activity: to do a load of laundry from sorting colours to folding
knowledge_domain: to do a load of laundry from sorting colours to folding
fact: Dots on the iron symbol set the highest safe iron setting: one dot is low, about 110 degrees Celsius, two is medium, about 150, and three is high, about 200.
story:
Joseph's parents had left for the weekend with one instruction: do your own laundry, and don't burn the house down. The second part sounded easy. The first part turned out to be a science project. The washer and dryer lived in the garage, wedged between a workbench and a tower of paint cans, and by Saturday afternoon Joseph had figured out sorting. Darks with darks, whites with whites, and the mystery pile that got washed cold because he didn't want to find out what would happen otherwise.

The trouble came at the ironing board. His robot costume shirt from the fall play was wrinkled, and he wanted it sharp for Monday, because Liliana had promised to bring her matching controller prop. He set the iron to cotton, which sounded like the strongest setting, and pressed the collar. The fabric made a small sighing noise. Where the iron had touched, the black nylon had gone shiny, a silver smear like frost on a window.

Noah, who had come over to "supervise," leaned in and reached for the shirt as if he could wipe the shine off with his thumb. Liliana intervened, stepping between them and the still-hot iron. "Nobody touches anything until we read something," she said. She flipped the shirt's tag while Joseph held his breath. Next to a little iron icon were two dots. "What does that even mean?" Joseph asked. They looked it up on Noah's phone, since Noah was the one who read cereal boxes out loud at lunch and knew the carbohydrate count of everything in Joseph's kitchen.

The answer made Joseph feel like the washer had shrunk his brain. Dots on the iron symbol set the highest safe iron setting. One dot was low, about 110 degrees Celsius. Two was medium, about 150. Three was high, about 200. His shirt had two dots, meaning 150, and cotton was way past that. He turned the dial down and pressed the sleeve carefully. No shine. The collar smear stayed, though. He tried dabbing it with a wet cloth, in vain, and finally draped his hoodie over it like a cape so it wouldn't show.

Monday morning, Liliana held up her controller and inspected him. "Nice cape," she said. "Very dramatic." Joseph shrugged. "The collar has a secret." "Everyone's collar has a secret," said Noah, and walked with them toward the bus.

activity: moving to a new town and leaving old friends behind
knowledge_domain: moving to a new town and leaving old friends behind
fact: In the United States, a permanent change of address filed with the Postal Service forwards First-Class Mail to the new address for 12 months.
story:
The new house smelled like paint and nothing else. Lauren walked from room to room with her shoes echoing on the bare floor, because the movers would not arrive until Thursday and there was no furniture to soften any sound. In her pocket, her phone held three texts from Jannat and two from Kaia, all from before the drive, when the signal still worked the way she was used to. Her father had filed the change of address form at the post office on their way out of town, and she kept thinking about that little pink slip of paper as if it were the only rope still tying her to home.

"Twelve months," she said out loud to the empty living room. The clerk had said the forwarding lasted twelve months for First-Class Mail, and only First-Class Mail, if the change was permanent. That part she had overheard while her father filled in their new address. Twelve months was a school year. A whole school year of letters that could still find her.

She sat on the floor of what would be her bedroom and opened her notebook. She had been designing a board game all summer, a prototype built from cardboard and bottle caps, and it was currently riding in a box somewhere on a truck between states. Jannat had been the one who told her the rules were too complicated, back in July. "Revise it," Jannat had said, sliding the fourth draft across the picnic table. "Or nobody but us will ever finish a game." Lauren had revised it twice more, and the newest version was the one packed away.

She texted Kaia: if you mail me the spare copy I left at your house, will it get here? Kaia replied with a photo of the manila envelope already sealed. They had guessed the same thing at the same time, like always.

Four days later, when the furniture had finally come and Lauren's bed was assembled, the envelope arrived with a yellow sticker bearing her new address. She turned it over and over, examining the sticker like evidence. First-Class Mail, forwarded, because her father had filed the permanent change of address. Twelve months, the clerk had said. She stuck the sticker in her notebook next to her game rules.

Inside the envelope was the prototype and a folded letter in Jannat's handwriting. "You left this at my house on purpose," it read, "so you would have to write back. Rule: every letter gets a letter." Lauren laughed, then read it twice more.

She found a stamp in her mother's wallet, spread the game board on the living room carpet, and began composing her reply right there, testing moves with bottle caps as she wrote. When she finished the first paragraph, she read it aloud to the empty room, just to hear a voice in it.

"Dear Jannat," she said. "Your move."

activity: making an art or craft project
knowledge_domain: making an art or craft project
fact: Oil paint does not dry by water evaporating; its oil slowly reacts with oxygen in the air, so an oil painting can take days or longer to dry to the touch.
story:
Andrew had been saving his Saturday afternoons all month for the community art studio's oil painting workshop, and today was the last class, which meant today his painting of the old lighthouse had to come home with him. He set the canvas on the rack by the window and studied it. The sky was good. The water was better than he expected. The lighthouse itself still needed its red stripes, and then, somehow, it had to survive a bus ride and a walk home in his hands.

"Mine's already dry," said Lilia, waving her small study of an apple near his ear. "I did mine thin. Watch." She touched a corner of her canvas with one finger and held it up to show him. Dry.

Andrew touched the corner of his own lighthouse. His fingertip came away shiny, and when he pressed a little harder, the paint gave, like butter left out on a warm counter. He frowned. He had not painted thickly on purpose, but the storm clouds had needed layer after layer, and the sky behind the beacon was laid on heavy because the first pass had looked wrong.

He tried the obvious fix. He carried the canvas over to the fan in the corner and set it in front of the breeze for ten minutes, then tested the corner again. Still tacky. Still shiny. He moved it under the warm studio lights. Nothing. It occurred to him that drying this paint was not like drying his gym clothes, which the fan would handle in an hour. Maybe there was no water in it to blow away at all.

"Mr. Ahmadi," Andrew called across the room, "is there any water in oil paint that has to dry out?"

Mr. Ahmadi came over, wiping his hands on a rag. "None to speak of," he said. "That's why you're stuck."

Kelly-Ann, who was washing her brushes at the sink, chimed in without turning around. "My cousin found this out the embarrassing way. She stacked her fresh painting face-down on her bed, and by morning it had a blanket print in the sky." Andrew laughed, then stopped laughing, because his own plan had been to carry the canvas flat against his chest, which was more or less the same disaster waiting for a bus.

So he thought about what the paint was actually doing instead of evaporating. If the oil was reacting with the air itself, then more air touching more surface might help. He carried the canvas back to the window, opened it wide, and balanced the painting upright on the sill with the wettest side facing the moving air, careful not to let anything lean against the face. It was naive to think it would be dry by five o'clock, and it wasn't. It was still soft three days later when he finally tested it at home, and the red stripes he added on Sunday took even longer, but that was fine now, because he knew what he was waiting for.

Lilia had solved the carrying problem for him before he left that day, though. She cut two cardboard squares from the scrap bin, drilled holes with a pencil, and tied them over the corners like a stretcher so nothing could touch the wet sky. "It looks like you're transporting a very fragile pizza," she said.

"Better than a blanket print," said Andrew, and he carried his lighthouse home through the wind, upright, like a boy escorting royalty.

activity: to solve linear equations with one variable by doing the same operation to both sides
knowledge_domain: to solve linear equations with one variable by doing the same operation to both sides
fact: To clear a fraction from an equation, multiply both sides by its denominator: if x divided by 3 equals 5, multiplying both sides by 3 gives x = 15.
story:
Scarlett spread three crumpled dollars and two quarters on the kitchen table and counted them twice, because the first count gave her a number she didn't like. "We're five dollars short," she said. "The pizza was thirty dollars, and this is twenty-five."

Rowan leaned over the money with the meticulous air of someone who did not believe her. "Everyone paid five," he said. "Me, Hendrix, you. And Hendrix's cousin paid five too."

"That's four people. Four times five is twenty." Hendrix drummed his pencil on the table. "Wait, it was supposed to be split three ways."

"Six ways," Rowan said. "Half slices count."

Scarlett pulled her math homework closer and stared at the problem Mr. Le had assigned: x divided by 3 equals 5. The numbers looked suspiciously familiar. "Okay, everyone paid five dollars each," she said slowly, "and there were three of them for that part. If each share is five, then..." She wrote x/3 = 5, then underneath it, 3 times x/3 equals 3 times 5.

"So x is fifteen," Hendrix said.

"Right, but that's only the first three people." Scarlett drew a box around the fifteen. Fatigue was creeping into her eyes from a full day of school, but she kept her pencil moving. "Three more people paid five each, so that's another fifteen. Fifteen and fifteen." She stopped. "That's the thirty."

Rowan mediated the dispute before it could start, laying one finger on her paper. "Prove it works. Go backward."

Scarlett tested it the way Mr. Le always nagged them to. Thirty dollars, three people on one side of the table, three on the other. Each side paid fifteen, and fifteen divided among three people is five dollars each. Everyone's share checked out. She slid the crumpled bills back across the table and re-counted, and this time she found a five folded inside Rowan's jacket pocket, where he had stuffed it during the walk home.

"That's why we were short," she said, holding it up. "Not the math."

Rowan grinned and dropped it into the pile. "Your equation was right the whole time."

"Thirty dollars, six people, five each." Scarlett copied the finished problem into her notebook and underlined the answer twice. At the door, Hendrix turned around. "Same time Thursday? My mom's ordering pizza again."

activity: to write a short story with correctly punctuated dialogue and a clear climax
knowledge_domain: to write a short story with correctly punctuated dialogue and a clear climax
fact: The protagonist is a story's main character, and the antagonist is the character or force working against them; their conflict drives the plot toward the climax.
story:
Georgia sat in the back of Ms. Hu's humid classroom on Friday afternoon, staring at the assignment sheet. Short story, five hundred words, due Monday morning. It had to have correctly punctuated dialogue and a clear climax. She had written three pages about a girl whose father forgot to pay the mortgage and had to sell the family farm, and now the whole thing felt like a long, sad puddle.

"It has no plot," said Anton, reading over her shoulder during the last ten minutes of class. "Stuff happens, then more stuff happens, then it's over."

"Thanks," said Georgia. "Very helpful."

Anton shrugged. "Ms. Hu said every story needs somebody fighting somebody. My story has a knight fighting a dragon. Boom. Done."

That night Georgia sprawled on her bedroom floor with a red pen. She circled her protagonist, whose name was Marisol, and tried to figure out who Marisol was fighting. Her father? He hadn't forgotten the mortgage on purpose. The bank? The bank didn't even show up in the story as a person. She remembered Ms. Hu saying something about how a protagonist and an antagonist couldn't both want the same thing, or nothing would ever move forward. The protagonist was a story's main character, and the antagonist was the character or force working against them; their conflict drove the plot toward the climax. Marisol, Georgia realized, wanted the farm saved. But the thing that kept slamming the gate shut was the blizzard that had frozen the pipes and ruined the pipes deal the buyer had wanted. Her antagonist wasn't a person at all. It was weather.

She tested the idea. If the snowstorm was the antagonist, then the climax had to be the moment Marisol faced it directly. Georgia cut two pages, kept a paragraph where the father said, "I can't fight the sky, kid," and added a scene where Marisol, at midnight, dragged heat tape out to the well house through knee-deep drifts, the wind shoving her sideways every third step. Then she went through the dialogue with her grammar sheet. New speaker, new paragraph. Comma inside the quotation marks. She fixed eleven mistakes and invented a rule to check her work: if she covered the dialogue tags with her finger and still knew who was talking, the punctuation was probably doing its job.

Saturday afternoon she found a message taped inside her locker, because Josephine refused to use her phone for serious business. The note read: "Dear Georgia. My antagonist is a hedge maze that eats people. My climax is the part where Anton's character gets lost in it, obviously. Meet me in the library at four and bring your draft, we will participate in peer review whether you like it or not. Yours, Josephine." Georgia laughed so hard a sixth grader turned around to stare.

In the library, Josephine read the blizzard scene twice. "This part gave me chills," she said. "The frost on the inside of the window. Good."

"You don't think it's weird that the villain is just snow?"

"The snow wants the pipes frozen. Marisol wants them working. That's the whole fight." Josephine slid the pages back. "My villain last year was my little brother, but he moved to Ohio, so I had to upgrade."

Georgia weighed that on the walk home. Last year she had written a story where nothing went wrong for anyone, because she had wanted everyone to be happy, and Ms. Hu had written "nice, but where's the trouble?" in green ink. Maybe she had been protecting her characters the way you'd protect a friend. Maybe you couldn't love a character and let a storm chase them at the same time. She still wasn't sure that was fair, but she kept walking anyway, and by the time she reached her block she was already drafting the last line in her head.

Monday morning she handed in the story, and Ms. Hu read the final page right there at the front of the room. She looked up and said, "The snow was winning the whole time. That's what made the ending work."

activity: to explain how the tilt of Earth's axis causes the seasons
knowledge_domain: to explain how the tilt of Earth's axis causes the seasons
fact: Around June 21, the noon Sun is directly overhead at the Tropic of Cancer; around December 21, it is directly overhead at the Tropic of Capricorn.
story:
Lily had one job on this camping trip: learn the seasons well enough to teach it to her class on Monday, and so far the only thing she understood was that the flashlight in the tent made terrible sunlight. Ronin sat cross-legged on a sleeping bag, holding the flashlight while Jaylen peeled an orange and Ms. Joshi, their neighbour who had organized the whole trip, stirred the camp stove outside.

"It's the distance," Ronin said. "Summer means we're closer to the Sun. My uncle told me."

"That can't be right," Lily said. "Then why is Australia having winter right now while we're swimming?"

Jaylen paused, orange halfway to his mouth. "Wait. Both halves can't be different distances. It's one ball."

Lily grabbed the small globe Ms. Joshi had packed for map practice. She spun it slowly, then stopped, because something on it had caught her eye before, at home, and she'd never followed it up. Two dotted lines curved around the globe, one above the equator and one below. "What are these?" she asked, mostly to herself. She tilted the globe the way Earth actually tilts, leaning the top away from her, and held her finger flat against a spot on the top dotted line. "Around June 21, the noon Sun is directly overhead here," she read from the label on the globe's stand. "That line's called the Tropic of Cancer."

She walked her flashlight-toting assistant through it. "Ronin, shine straight down on my finger."

He aimed. The light hit her fingertip and spread into a small, bright circle on the globe. "Now shine on the same spot, but hold the flashlight level with the equator," she said, tilting the globe back the other way. The beam now struck at a slant, and the bright circle stretched into a long, pale oval.

"It spreads out," Jaylen said, leaning in. "Same light, more ground. So it's weaker."

"And down here," Lily said, moving her finger to the lower dotted line, "around December 21 the noon Sun is directly overhead at the Tropic of Capricorn. It's their turn for the straight-down light." She looked up. "That's why their seasons are backwards. It's not distance at all. It's the tilt, and which half gets the direct beam."

Ronin set the flashlight down slowly. "Okay," he said. "My uncle is going to hear about this."

Ms. Joshi ducked her head into the tent, saw the globe glowing under the flashlight like a tiny sunlit planet, and smiled. "Whatever this is," she said, "can you demonstrate it at breakfast? Because I want to see it too."

activity: the idea that people interpret the same events and ideas differently
knowledge_domain: the idea that people interpret the same events and ideas differently
fact: In the Sally-Anne test, first used in 1985, children from about age four usually say a character will look where she left her marble, not where it was moved while she was away.
story:
Ms. Brown started the discussion by putting a question on the board, which everyone agreed was a bad sign. "Sally puts her marble in her basket and goes outside," she said. "While she's out, her sister moves the marble to a box. Sally comes back. Where will she look for her marble?"

"In the box," said Matt, without raising his hand. "It's in the box."

Carolina turned around in her seat. "That's not what the question asked. She'll look in the basket, because that's where she left it."

"It's in the box," Matt said again, slowly, as if Carolina might not have heard the first time. "Looking in the basket would be a waste of her time."

Jack had been half listening, but now he sat up, because he had a four-year-old cousin, Lily, and last weekend Lily had searched the whole kitchen for her hair clipper even though their uncle had moved it to the bathroom while she was in the garden. Jack had assumed she was just being dramatic, which was Lily's usual setting. Now he wasn't so sure. Maybe Lily genuinely expected it to be where she'd left it, the way Matt genuinely expected Sally to look in the box.

"Jack," said Ms. Brown, "you're monitoring the window instead of us."

"Sorry." He leaned forward. "I think it depends how old Sally is. The question doesn't say."

Ms. Brown looked mildly pleased, which was annoying because it meant she'd been waiting for that. "This is called the Sally-Anne test," she said. "It was first used in 1985. Children from about age four usually say Sally will look in the basket, where she left her marble, not the box where it was moved while she was away." She wrote the two words on the board and let them sit there.

Matt frowned at the board as if it had personally misled him. "So kids under four say the box? That's what I said."

"You sound like a three-year-old," Carolina said, not unkindly.

"I sound like someone who knows where the marble is."

"That's exactly the problem," Jack said. The idea was arriving in his head fully formed, like it had been waiting outside. "Sally doesn't know where the marble is. She believes something that's wrong, and she'll act on it anyway. Lily isn't dramatic. She just thinks the world still matches what she saw last."

"You're going to test that on her, aren't you," Carolina said.

"Saturday. I'll hide her stuffed rabbit somewhere while she's out of the room and see where she looks." He paused. "If she cries, that's on the two of you."

Ms. Brown collected the critiques they'd written about their debate arguments, and Jack watched her stack the papers instead of handing them back. "Saturday," Carolina whispered as the bell rang. "Bring the rabbit back."

activity: the difference between an opinion and a claim that can be checked
knowledge_domain: the difference between an opinion and a claim that can be checked
fact: Professional fact-checkers use lateral reading: instead of judging a website by its own pages, they open new tabs to see what other sources say about it.
story:
Simon had forty dollars saved from mowing lawns, and he was about to spend it on a bottle of "OceanGuard Xtreme," a miracle cleaner that promised to make a boat's hull shine like glass with one wipe. His dad had been grumbling about the green slime on the hull of their little fishing boat all summer, and Simon wanted to surprise him.

The website looked amazing. Blue water, a smiling scientist in a lab coat, and five gold stars under the words "Rated the number one hull cleaner in America." Simon reached for his mom's credit card, which he was allowed to use for birthday presents only, then stopped. Something felt off, but he couldn't say what. He texted his friend Ares.

"Check this site," Ares replied. "It looks so official." Tom, their classmate, messaged a minute later: "Order it before the sale ends!" But Simon kept staring at the scientist's photo. His mom had taught him one rule: when a page tells you how great it is, don't just sit there reading more of the same page. So he tried something. He opened a new tab and typed the company's name plus the word "review." Then another tab, and another, like he was sliding sideways across the internet instead of deeper into it.

The first new tab showed a news article: OceanGuard Xtreme was made by a company called Seabright Products, which also ran the review site that gave it five stars. The "scientist" turned out to be a stock photo. In a third tab, a boating forum was full of complaints about streaky, discolored hulls. Simon sat back. The website's own words and the rest of the internet ran in two parallel directions, and only one of them could be true.

"Lateral reading," Ares said when Simon told him. "My cousin calls it that. You read sideways, not down." Ms. De Vries, their neighbor, was watering her tomatoes over the fence, and when she heard the story she laughed. "So you saved your forty dollars by opening tabs instead of trusting tabs."

Simon revised his plan that evening. He looked up ordinary marine soap, checked three separate sites that had nothing to do with the seller, and found one for twelve dollars with real reviews from people who posted photos of their own boats. He ordered it. On Saturday he scrubbed the hull until his arms ached and the green slime came away in long slippery sheets, and his dad stood at the dock holding a cold drink, staring at the gleam.

"You did this?" his dad asked.

Simon wrung out the sponge and grinned. "I did my research."

activity: to read the rights listed in their country's constitution or charter and explain one in their own words
knowledge_domain: to read the rights listed in their country's constitution or charter and explain one in their own words
fact: The first ten amendments to the United States Constitution are called the Bill of Rights, and they were ratified in 1791.
story:
Nathaniel spread the photocopy of the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms across the kitchen table and stared at section after section until the words blurred together. Ms. Murphy had assigned each student one right to explain in their own words tomorrow, and his was section 8, protection against unreasonable search. The problem was that every time he tried to put it into his own words, he just copied the textbook's words instead.

"Still stuck?" his mother asked, setting a glass of milk beside him.

"Sort of," he said. "I know what it says. I just can't say it differently."

At dinner he barely touched his pasta, and after dinner he called Sophie, because Sophie's grandmother lived in Chicago and Sophie knew things about the United States that nobody else in class did. "Here's an idea," she said over video. "Don't look at our Charter for a minute. My grandma has a copy of their constitution on her wall. She says the first ten amendments are called the Bill of Rights, and they were ratified in 1791."

"That's ancient," Nathaniel said. "Older than Canada."

"So compare them," Sophie said. "If you look through the lens of their Bill of Rights, our section might look different. Like trying on someone else's glasses." She held up her own notebook, where she had scribbled notes from her grandmother's last visit.

Nathaniel remembered that visit, back in October. He had been at Sophie's house when her grandmother unfolded a brittle photocopy and pointed to the fourth amendment, reading aloud about searches and warrants while Sophie translated it into plainer language for him. "It basically means the police can't just barge in and rummage through your stuff," Sophie had said then, "without a good reason they can show." He had nodded, not realizing he would need that sentence six months later.

He hung up, found the fourth amendment online, and laid it beside section 8 of the Charter. He read one, then the other, then the first again. They were cousins, not twins. He grabbed a fresh sheet of paper and wrote, "Nobody gets to search you or your things just because they feel like it. They need a real reason, and usually permission from a judge." He read it out loud to the empty kitchen. It sounded like a person talking, not a textbook.

At school the next morning, Ms. Murphy walked the rows while students practiced. When she stopped at his desk, Nathaniel pushed his paper toward her before his courage could leak away. She read it, then read it again, and tapped the margin with one finger.

"Whose words are these?" she asked.

"Mine," he said. "But I tested them. I compared ours with the American one, the fourth amendment, because their Bill of Rights was ratified in 1791 and it's been argued about for centuries. If my version worked on both, I figured it was the right idea, not just the wording." He paused. "Also Sophie helped. Her grandma has the actual document framed on her wall."

Ms. Murphy smiled and moved on, and Nathaniel noticed Cataleya across the aisle, frowning at a page covered in crossed-out sentences. He slid his milk carton over to her along with a sticky note that said, "Try saying it to a six-year-old. That's what fixed mine." Cataleya read the note, grinned, and started whispering her right to an imaginary little brother.

At lunch she found him by the water fountain. "It worked," she said. "Freedom of expression, kid version: you're allowed to say what you think, and nobody's immune from hearing stuff they don't like."

activity: to improvise a blues solo over a twelve-bar chord progression
knowledge_domain: to improvise a blues solo over a twelve-bar chord progression
fact: A basic twelve-bar blues uses three chords, built on the first, fourth and fifth notes of the scale and written as the I, IV and V chords.
story:
The church basement smelled like coffee and old hymnals, and the folding chairs had been pushed back to make room for the jam session that met there every Saturday afternoon. Isabelle tuned her guitar while Nika, who played a borrowed keyboard, leaned over and pointed at the chord chart Mr. Chea had taped to the piano.

"Everyone keeps saying one-four-five," Nika whispered. "What does that even mean?"

Before Isabelle could shrug, the keyboard player from the earlier band, a teenager with a trombone case, answered on his way to the snack table. "It means the three chords. One, four and five. Built on the first, fourth and fifth notes of the scale, so people just write them as the I, the IV and the V." He grabbed a cookie and kept walking.

Isabelle traced the chart with her finger. The line of twelve bars went I, I, I, I, IV, IV, I, I, V, IV, I, I. Three chords, then, cycling around and around, the same pattern every time through. She had been soloing by guessing, and it had sounded like a siege on everyone's ears, notes flung at random until the whole thing collapsed. Maybe the guessing wasn't the problem. Maybe she just didn't know where the ground was.

"Here's my idea," she told Nika while the drummer counted in the band before theirs. "During the I bars, I only pick notes that live inside the I chord. When it switches to the IV, I switch too. I follow the chords instead of fighting them."

"That's it?" Nika said.

"That's the test. If it works, I'll hear it."

Their turn came. The bass player nodded at her, the drummer tapped his sticks together, and the twelve bars rolled past like water through a porous wall, every gap letting the sound leak into the next measure. Isabelle stayed small at first, landing on one safe note per chord change, then two, then a little climb from the V chord right when the pattern came back around to the I. It fit. It actually fit, the way a key fits a lock she had been jabbing at blindly.

When the song ended, Mr. Chea gave her a thumbs up from his chair by the door.

"Now more notes," Nika said, already flipping her music back to the start. "Same idea, braver fingers."

Isabelle laughed and set her pick on the strings, waiting for the count.

activity: to measure the speed of a rolling ball from distance and time and draw a distance-time graph
knowledge_domain: to measure the speed of a rolling ball from distance and time and draw a distance-time graph
fact: On a distance-time graph, time goes along the horizontal axis and distance goes up the vertical axis.
story:
Elizabeth had until Sunday night to turn her backyard into a science lab, which was a problem because her backyard was mainly a place where the dog buried things. The assignment sheet from Mr. Pritchard said: measure the speed of a rolling ball, then draw a distance-time graph. Speed was easy, Layton had told her. You rolled the ball, you timed it, you divided. The graph was the part nobody had explained.

She set it up anyway. Hope stood at the top of the slope with the soccer ball and a borrowed stopwatch, and Elizabeth knelt at the bottom with a tape measure, a clipboard, and the diligence of someone who had already lost points on two assignments this term. "On three," Hope called. "One, two, three." The ball came down the grass, wobbling around a bare patch where the dog had been energetic, and Elizabeth marked where it stopped. Fifteen seconds, twelve metres. Then ten. Then eight. Hope wrote the numbers in her notebook and squinted at the grass. "This is basically an ecosystem down here. There's a whole city of ants judging us."

They counted six rolls before the rain started, and Hope had to go home for dinner, so the graph part fell to Elizabeth alone at the kitchen table. She drew her axes, plotted the points, and sat back. The line went straight up, nearly vertical, which would mean the ball had covered the whole yard in about one second. That was wrong. She checked her division, the numbers, everything twice. Then she looked at her axes. She had put distance along the bottom and time up the side.

She texted Hope, because Hope's older sister had done this unit last year.

Hope's reply came back a minute later: "you did what my sister did lol. time along the bottom. distance goes up. swap it and see."

Elizabeth flipped the paper over and drew it again, time along the horizontal axis, distance up the vertical one. This time the points climbed in a slow, sensible line. She leaned back and looked at it. So that was what the graph was for. The numbers on the clipboard were just numbers, but this line, this slope, could signify speed itself, the whole afternoon of rolling a ball around a dog-damaged yard compressed into one thin diagonal pencil mark.

She was still holding the paper up to the kitchen light when her mother came in. "What's that supposed to be?"

"The backyard," Elizabeth said. "Sort of."

activity: to play a piece with dynamics and tempo changes in a band or on the piano
knowledge_domain: to play a piece with dynamics and tempo changes in a band or on the piano
fact: The piano's full name is pianoforte, meaning soft-loud, because the player can make notes soft or loud by how hard the keys are struck.
story:
George had three days to learn the middle section of "The Lonely Road," and the piano at Marilou's house was the only one he could get to after school. He set his sheet music on the rack while Marilou's grandmother set down two plates of crackers and cheese without a word. The deadline was real: on Friday, the three of them, George, Marilou and Kaliyah, were playing the piece for Ms. Kapoor's music class as a small ensemble, and George had the solo.

"Play it once so we can hear the damage," Marilou said, sitting on the couch with Kaliyah.

George played. The notes were right, every one of them, but Kaliyah winced at the same moment Marilou did.

"It's flat," Kaliyah said. "Not the pitch. The whole thing. It's like a robot reading a grocery list."

"The sheet says forte here and piano here," George said, tapping the page. "I did that. Loud, then soft."

Marilou came over and stood behind him. "It's more than loud and soft. It's like the difference between someone yelling 'look out' and someone whispering 'look out.' Same word, different everything."

George played the loud part again and watched his own finger hit the key. Then he played it the way he'd been playing, and he noticed something. When he played loud, he struck fast and pulled his hand back fast, so each note cut off sharp. When he played soft, he slowed down so much that the notes blurred together and the tempo dragged. He was changing two things at once instead of one.

"Wait," he said. "Do it again but slow," Marilou said, but George was already trying something. He kept his tempo steady, counting one-two-three-four under his breath like a heartbeat, and changed only how hard his fingers came down. The loud part came out full and round instead of sharp. The soft part stayed light but kept its place in the rhythm, like footsteps instead of a puddle.

"What did you change?" Kaliyah asked, coming to stand at the end of the piano.

"How hard I hit. Not how fast. My cousin told me the piano's full name is pianoforte. It means soft-loud, because the player can make notes soft or loud by how hard the keys are struck." He shrugged. "I thought that was just a history thing. It's actually the whole instruction manual."

Marilou's grandmother, passing through with a watering can for the ferns, paused at the word pianoforte and smiled, but said nothing.

George ran the section six more times. By the fourth time his hands knew the difference on their own, and by the sixth Kaliyah had stopped wincing and started nodding her head in time. When he finished, the last soft note hung in the room and faded into the sound of the grandfather clock ticking in the hallway.

"Friday," Kaliyah said. "We're going to be exceptional."

George retrieved his sheet music from the rack, folded it into his backpack, and ate every cracker on his plate.

activity: to read the periodic table and find the number of protons in an element from its atomic number
knowledge_domain: to read the periodic table and find the number of protons in an element from its atomic number
fact: The vertical columns of the periodic table are called groups, and elements in the same group tend to have similar chemical properties.
story:
Aurora spread her science homework across her grandmother's kitchen table, which smelled like cardamom and dish soap. The worksheet wanted her to find the number of protons in gold, and the periodic table in her textbook was so small she had to squint. Her grandfather slid a huge laminated chart out from behind the refrigerator, where it had apparently lived for years. "Your grandmother used it for agriculture," he said. "Soil chemistry. Big print helps old eyes."

The gold square said 79 in the corner. Aurora copied that onto her worksheet and then stopped, pencil hovering. How was she supposed to know that 79 meant protons and not something else, like the weight? She couldn't see a proton. Nobody could. She flipped through the textbook until she found the line that said the atomic number was the number of protons, and she felt the small click of it, like a key finding its lock. Then she noticed something stranger. Helium, neon, and argon were stacked in a perfect column on the far right, like cans on a supermarket shelf.

"Grandpa, why are these three in a line?" she asked.

He leaned over the chart. "The vertical columns are called groups," he said, and went back to his tea.

Groups. Aurora traced the column with her finger, down through krypton and xenon. Her teacher, Ms. Park, had said something in class that Aurora had half ignored, something about elements that behave alike. If the chart grouped them on purpose, maybe the whole table was sorted by behavior, not just by number. She tested it on the left side: lithium, sodium, and potassium all sat in one column, and she remembered a demonstration where sodium and potassium had both skittered across water like water striders. Same column, same trick. She wrote in her notebook, columns mean similar properties, and underlined it twice, feeling like a spy who has cracked part of a code.

Then she texted her friend Jaiveer, who was obstinate about being right and would argue about anything, even lunch.

"Question," she typed. "Nitrogen and phosphorus are in the same group. Do you think they act alike, yes or no?"

His reply came back in a long message that read almost like a letter. "Dear Aurora, no, because they are different colors and different names and phosphorus starts with P, which proves nothing connects them. Also your chart is probably from the refrigerator era. Sincerely, Jaiveer." She laughed so hard her grandmother called from the garden to ask who was hurt.

Aurora wrote back, "They're in the same column, so same group, so they probably behave similarly. Check what Mrs. Park said about plant fertilizer. Nitrogen AND phosphorus. Both feed plants. Coincidence? The chart says no." She hit send before she could abandon her argument, then dragged the huge chart to the window where the light was better and started hunting for the next pattern, her pencil ticking down column seventeen like a woodpecker.

activity: to run an eight-hundred-metre race pacing the first lap so there is energy for the second
knowledge_domain: to run an eight-hundred-metre race pacing the first lap so there is energy for the second
fact: Sprinting the first lap faster than a pace you can hold uses up quick anaerobic energy early, so the runner usually slows sharply on the second lap.
story:
Jacob had lost the eight hundred metres the same way three times, and he could not figure out why. Each race he led the first lap, arms pumping, the crowd loud behind him, and each time the second lap felt like running through wet sand. He decided the problem was hidden somewhere in the race itself, so at Thursday practice he asked Mr. Dlamini if he could run a time trial while Lilah watched from the fence.

"You look strong until the bend," Lilah reported afterward, notebook in hand. "Then it's like somebody turns a valve and lets all your speed out." She tapped her pencil against the page. "The guys you beat at the two hundred mark catch you on the final straight. Every single time." Jacob studied her numbers. His first lap was always faster than anything he could hold for two laps, and his second lap was always much slower. The pattern was there in the splits, plain as footprints.

"So what if the first lap is the trap?" he said. "What if going out fast is exactly what ruins the second lap?" It seemed backwards. Everyone wanted the lead. But he had a simple test: run the first lap slower on purpose, deliberately, even if runners passed him, and see what was left at the end. He felt cautiously optimistic about it, though not certain, because slowing down on purpose felt like admitting defeat before the race had even started.

At the county meet, Lilah was in his heat, and she wanted this one badly. Her older sister had held the school record, and she had said twice that morning she was going to take it. The gun went off and she surged to the front immediately, three metres clear by the first bend, exactly the way Jacob used to. He stayed back, flat and even, counting his steps, letting the pack pull away while he held a pace he knew he could repeat.

The bell rang for the final lap and the race turned. Lilah's stride shortened on the back straight; the gap that had looked uncatchable began to close, then to vanish. Jacob swung wide on the last bend, and on the final straight he passed her, then passed the boy in front of her too, and crossed the line second overall with his fastest time ever. He walked back up the track, hands on his head, breathing hard. Lilah was bent over the infield grass.

"You found it," she said. "The first lap. Go out faster than you can hold, and the second lap just dies."

Jacob sat down beside her in the cool grass. "Next time," he said, "count your splits like you counted mine."

activity: to build a web page with HTML and style it with CSS so the heading is centred
knowledge_domain: to build a web page with HTML and style it with CSS so the heading is centred
fact: The CSS rule h1 { text-align: center; } centres the text of every top-level heading on the page.
story:
Alex had twenty minutes before the judges came around, and the team's homepage still looked wrong. The robotics club had built a small website for their competition booth, a page with photos of their robot, a build log, and a big heading at the top. The heading hugged the left edge like it was trying to hide, while everything else sat neatly in the middle. Ms. Bekele, who was running the booth check-in, had already walked past twice.

"It looks like it's apologizing for being there," said Rayane, squinting at the laptop screen.

"I know," Alex said. Last year he had skipped the coding workshop because he thought HTML was boring, and now that choice sat in his stomach like a swallowed bolt. He'd rather be tightening a gear. Instead he was typing words he only half understood between two curly brackets.

Camilla leaned over his shoulder. "Try the thing from the practice page. You wrote it there, remember? The one with the braces."

Alex found it in his notes: h1 { text-align: center; }. He typed it in, saved, and refreshed the page. The main heading slid to the middle of the screen, and Rayane actually clapped. But something else had moved too. Their build log page, which they had linked from the homepage, now had every big title sitting in its centre as well, including one they had wanted on the left under the photo captions.

"That rule changed all of them," Alex said slowly. He scrolled through the pages to check. Every top-level heading, every single one marked h1, had shifted to the centre. It wasn't a one-time fix. It was a rule the whole page obeyed.

"So we either change those headings to a different level," Camilla said, "or we let them all be centred."

They voted on it, quick and quiet, and the result was unanimous: centre everything, it looked cleaner anyway. Alex fixed the two stray headings by re-tagging them, saved, and watched the page settle.

"Ten minutes," Ms. Bekele called from the doorway, tapping her watch. "Judges are circulating through the gym. Make sure your screens are on."

Alex generated a QR code for the site and taped it to the front of the booth. Their robot, nicknamed Recession because they'd built it entirely from parts scavenged after the club's budget got cut, waited beside it with its arm raised.

The first judge stopped, scanned the code, and looked at her tablet. "Nice page," she said. "Who did the web work?"

Alex raised his hand. "Still learning," he said. "But the heading's centred."

activity: to explain how nicotine causes addiction in the brain's reward pathway
knowledge_domain: to explain how nicotine causes addiction in the brain's reward pathway
fact: The brain keeps developing until about age 25, which makes young people more vulnerable to nicotine addiction than adults.
story:
Alexander sat in the dentist's waiting room next to Cheikh, who kept glancing at his backpack like it contained something illegal, which, Alexander realized, it might. The receptionist had called Alexander's name and then said there was a delay, so both boys were stuck with the fish tank and a rack of pamphlets. Alexander had already read the one about flossing twice.

"Okay, don't freak out," Cheikh whispered. He unzipped the front pocket just enough to show a slim metal tube. "My cousin gave it to me. Mango flavor. I was going to try it after, you know, in the parking lot. Come with me?"

Alexander picked up another pamphlet, mostly to have something in his hands. This one was about tobacco, and it had a diagram inside: a drawing of a brain with an arrow pointing to a shaded strip along the bottom labeled reward pathway. He read that nicotine landed on that strip and made it fire, releasing a chemical that felt good. The brain noticed the good feeling, then adjusted itself so that ordinary things, like lunch or a joke, didn't hit the same way anymore. You needed more nicotine just to feel normal. Alexander read it twice. The mechanism was invisible, the same way gravity was invisible, but the pamphlet's arrow made him feel like he could almost see it.

"That's why it hooks people," he said slowly. "It doesn't just feel good. It rewires the part that decides what feels good." He tapped the diagram. "It's like a shortcut that violates every other road. Your brain stops using the normal routes because the shortcut is faster."

Cheikh looked at the tube in his hand. "It's just mango."

"Here's the thing." Alexander flipped the page, and there it was, in bold: the brain keeps developing until about age 25, which makes young people more vulnerable to nicotine addiction than adults. He stared at the sentence. So the rewiring didn't happen in a finished brain; it happened in a construction site. Their age wasn't just a detail. It was the whole reason the shortcut could get paved so easily.

The door opened and a man in scrubs, Mr. Grant, the dentist, called, "Alexander? Sorry for the wait." Alexander stood up, then paused.

"Mr. Grant, one question. This pamphlet says nicotine rewires the reward pathway. That's real? Not just a scare thing?"

"As real as your molars," Mr. Grant said. "You, especially, at your age. I've had patients your age who got hooked in months."

Cheikh zipped the pocket shut with a small snap. "Fine," he said, standing too. "But you owe me, because I am absolutely telling my cousin his mango brain rewirer violated my trust." He handed the tube to Mr. Grant like it was a dead fish.

Mr. Grant dropped it in the sharps container by the door. "Alexander, chair two. And you," he said to Cheikh, "sit back down, you're next."

activity: getting a first phone and learning to use it responsibly
knowledge_domain: getting a first phone and learning to use it responsibly
fact: The phone Martin Cooper used for the first handheld cell phone call weighed about 1.1 kilograms (2.5 pounds).
story:
The box sat on Lyric's kitchen table between a bowl of tangerines and a half-finished crossword. Samuel had carried it from his own house three doors down, because his mother had said he could open it at Lyric's, where there was better light and fewer little brothers.

"It's heavy for a phone," Lyric said, tipping the box with one finger.

"It's mostly packaging." Samuel cut the tape and lifted out the phone, which weighed almost nothing in his palm. Lyric's grandfather, who was doing the crossword, looked over his glasses and laughed.

"Light," he said. "You kids think this is a phone. The first handheld cell phone call weighed about 1.1 kilograms. Two and a half pounds. Like carrying a bag of sugar."

"Who carried it?" Samuel asked.

"A man named Martin Cooper. Held that thing up to his ear in the middle of a street." The grandfather went back to seven across.

Samuel turned the phone over. His mother had set it up before wrapping it, but she had left him a note: no more than one hour a day, and she could see how much he used it. He wanted more than an hour, at least this first week, and he suspected there was a way around the rule. A rule run by software had to have a crack somewhere. He decided to test it.

He opened the settings and looked for the timer. There it was, a screen-time limit with his mother's password on it. He tried changing the clock on the phone, setting it ahead three hours, thinking the phone might think the day was over. Nothing happened. He tried turning the limit off. It asked for the password again.

"Give up?" Lyric said, peeling a tangerine.

"One more idea." Samuel put the phone in airplane mode and played the racing game that was already downloaded. The minutes ticked up in the corner anyway. He sighed and switched it off.

That evening his mother texted him from the kitchen, three doors away: "Nice try, clock boy." She had a report too, apparently. He walked home with the phone in his pocket, feeling its small weight, and found her at the counter.

"You changed the time," she said.

"I wanted to know if it would work."

"And now you know." She slid a sheet of paper across the counter. "New deal. One hour a day, but you can earn ten extra minutes by charging it in the kitchen overnight. Every night it's in there, ten minutes. It's about stamina, not tricks."

"That's a weird use of stamina."

"Phones die without it. So do deals." She held out her hand, and he shook it.

He carried the phone back to Lyric's the next morning, held it out flat on his palm like a scale. "Guess what this weighs."

"Nothing," Lyric said.

"About point one seven kilograms," Samuel said. "I weighed it on the kitchen scale. Grandpa's phone was more than six times heavier." He put it in his pocket. "I'll earn my extra minutes tonight."

activity: to write a Python program that asks for a number and prints whether it is prime
knowledge_domain: to write a Python program that asks for a number and prints whether it is prime
fact: A Python for loop can have an else block that runs only if the loop finished without reaching break, which fits 'no divisor found, so the number is prime'.
story:
Rebecca sat cross-legged on the living room rug with her laptop balanced on a dictionary, because the coffee table had been claimed by a monopoly game that Adam and Eloise had refused to pause. "Just one trade," Adam had said forty minutes ago. The board was still spread out, and Eloise was arranging her little green houses into a row like a fence.

Rebecca had homework due Monday: a Python program that asks for a number and prints whether it is prime. She had managed the first part fine. The program asked for a number, and she typed one in, and the computer waited politely, the cursor blinking in the black window. Then the program was supposed to decide, and there everything fell apart.

She wrote a loop that tried every possible divisor, and when it found one she printed "not prime" and used break to escape. But how did the program know, afterward, whether it had broken out or just run out of numbers to try? She stared at the screen, tapped the touchpad, and tried keeping a separate flag variable called found. It worked, sort of, but it looked lumpy, like a sweater with an extra sleeve.

She thought back to the coding camp last summer. Ms. Virtanen, the mentor, had leaned over their table while everyone was stuck on exactly this kind of problem, and she had said, "You can put an else block on the for loop itself." Nobody at the table had known that. "It runs only if the loop finished without reaching break," she'd added, and then she'd moved on to help the next table, leaving them all blinking at each other. Rebecca remembered Eloise whispering, "Loops have secrets," and Adam writing it on his hand in pen.

Back on the rug, Rebecca deleted her lumpy flag variable. She lined up the for loop, the break inside it, and then, right at the same level as the for, she wrote else: and under it, print("prime"). Her heart did a small hop as she pressed run.

She typed 7. "prime." She typed 9. "not prime." She typed 15, then 11, then 23, leaning closer each time.

Eloise abandoned the monopoly board and slid across the rug. "What's it doing?"

"Deciding if numbers are prime," Rebecca said. "Watch." She typed 25, and the screen said "not prime," and she grinned so hard her cheeks hurt.

Adam peered over her shoulder, one hand still full of orange money. "Do four next."

She typed 4. The cursor blinked once, and the answer appeared in small white letters: "not prime."

"Again," Adam said, holding out his hand for the keyboard. "My turn, my turn."

activity: planting a vegetable garden and watching it grow
knowledge_domain: planting a vegetable garden and watching it grow
fact: Squash plants grow separate male and female flowers, and only a female flower, which has a tiny fruit at its base, can grow into a squash after being pollinated.
story:
Carson had been waiting all summer for squash, and now it was the last week of July and he had none. The plants in the corner of Ms. Yamamoto's garden were enormous, with leaves like green umbrellas and more flowers than he could count. He crouched between the rows and picked one, then another, comparing them under the Saturday sun.

"Still nothing?" Myles called from the tomato stakes, where he was supposed to be tying vines and was instead eating cherry tomatoes like popcorn.

"Look at these," Carson said, holding up both flowers. "This one has a little bump under the petals, like a tiny squash already started. This one doesn't." He turned them slowly, as if the difference might vanish if he stared too hard.

Macie came over, wiping dirt off her knees. "So?"

"So the plant makes two kinds of flowers. That's weird." He set the smooth-stemmed one down and kept the bumpy one. "Why would some flowers come with a fruit already attached and some come with nothing?"

Ms. Yamamoto, hauling a watering can past the beans, paused long enough to say, "Hand-pollinating takes a soft brush, if you ever need one," and kept walking, as if that were a completely normal sentence.

Carson thought about the zucchini at the garden center in June, when he had picked out his seedlings. He remembered standing in the crowded aisle while Macie argued that tomatoes were more versatile, good for sandwiches and sauce and skewers, and he had insisted squash was better because one plant made so much food. He had imagined baskets of it. He had not imagined a plant that flowered and flowered and produced nothing at all.

He frowned at the rows. "Macie. The flowers with no bump. What if they're the boy ones?" He could not see any reason a plant would need two kinds, but he could perceive a pattern when it was sitting in his palm, and the pattern was that every flower on the plant was one or the other, never both.

"So the bumpy ones are girls," Macie said. "And only girls can turn into squash. The boys just... help."

"That's what I think. And I think nobody's helping." He had seen almost no bees all week, maybe because the neighbors had sprayed their lawn. He cupped the bumpy flower gently in one hand.

Myles finally wandered over, and the three of them called a truce on the tomato debate long enough to try Ms. Yamamoto's advice. Carson swirled a small paintbrush inside a smooth-stemmed flower until the bristles looked dusty gold, then touched it to the center of a bumpy one, right above the tiny fruit.

He marked the stem with a twist tie so he would know which one it was.

Four mornings later Carson ran to the garden before breakfast, knelt down, and found the twist tie. Behind it, fat and firm and unmistakable, sat a zucchini as long as his hand.

"Told you," he shouted toward the tomatoes, and Macie and Myles came running.

activity: to look at onion skin cells under a microscope and label the cell wall, membrane and nucleus
knowledge_domain: to look at onion skin cells under a microscope and label the cell wall, membrane and nucleus
fact: The nucleus in an onion cell shows up as a small, round, darker spot, and it holds the cell's genetic material, DNA.
story:
Asher set the microscope on the picnic table and checked twice that nobody had bumped it. His grandfather had lent it to him on one condition, that it came back perfect, and last summer Asher had broken that same grandfather's binoculars by leaving them on the porch rail in the rain. He was not going to feel that sick feeling again.

Haider had brought the onion, half of one wrapped in tinfoil from his mother's kitchen. Landen had the assignment sheet folded into his pocket, slightly damp from the sprinkler. Ms. Brennan had assigned the project for Monday, a drawing of onion skin cells with three labels, and Asher had invited them over because his backyard was the only place with a microscope.

They peeled a thin layer of skin off the onion, thin enough to almost see through, and laid it on a slide with a drop of water. Asher turned the fine focus knob one slow revolution at a time, and the blur resolved into rows of brick-shaped cells, each one outlined like a garden plot with fences.

"There," Landen said. "Cell wall, that's the outer edge. And the membrane, it's right inside the wall, kind of a second line."

"That leaves the nucleus," Haider said. He leaned in and scrutinized the slide, squinting at one cell after another. "But all I see is a little dark dot in each one. Is that part of the cell, or did we get dirt in there?"

"Every single cell has one," Asher said slowly. "If it were dirt, it would show up in random places. It's in the same spot, or close to it, every time."

Landen wasn't convinced. "Dirt could be everywhere too."

Asher thought about the binoculars, about how he had assumed they were fine sitting there and never checked. He was not going to label something without checking this time. "Watch," he said. He nudged the slide a fraction to the left with the corner of the coverslip, careful not to smear it. The cells shifted. The dark dots shifted with them, staying inside their own cells like passengers on a moving bus. Real dirt would have slid or stayed behind. He nudged it back and the dots rode along again.

"Okay," Landen said, pulling out the assignment sheet. "So the dot is the nucleus." He wrote it on the drawing, arrow pointing to a small round spot he had shaded darker than the rest of the cell. Haider copied the label onto his own drawing, then paused.

"It holds the DNA," Haider said. "That's what Ms. Brennan told us Tuesday. The genetic material, the stuff that makes an onion an onion."

"That's the whole fact then," Asher said. He felt the good kind of proud, the kind that came after checking instead of before. He looked at the microscope sitting safe on the table, still in one piece, and then at the sky, which had gone the grey that usually meant rain.

"Inside," he said, picking it up with both hands. "Right now."

activity: cooking or baking a meal for the family
knowledge_domain: cooking or baking a meal for the family
fact: Water should never be poured on a grease fire, because it turns to steam instantly and spreads the burning oil; turning off the heat and covering the pan with a lid smothers it.
story:
Anna set the portable burner on the picnic table at the back of the house, because tonight she was making dinner all by herself, her one real chance before her grandmother arrived on Saturday. She had chosen fried rice, and she had chosen it on purpose, since the recipe app she used had a whole database of meals rated by difficulty, and this one had three stars. Gwen sat cross-legged on the grass nearby, filming short videos for their class project on cooking safety. "I need something dramatic," Gwen said. "Nobody wants to watch somebody stir rice."

"I'm not here to make your video better," Anna said, trying to sound assertive, though her voice wobbled. "I'm here to make dinner." Gwen shrugged and kept filming anyway.

The bacon went into the pan first, and Anna turned the heat up to make it finish faster, which she immediately regretted. Grease popped, and the oil in one corner caught, a small orange tongue of flame curling up the side of the pan. Anna's hand shot toward the pitcher of water she had set out for the rice.

Gwen screamed, "Don't! My uncle poured water on one at our cookout and the whole pan went up in a wall of fire." Anna froze, pitcher in the air. Her mind raced back to the campout last summer, when her dad had slid a lid over a flaring pan instead of reaching for the water, calm as anything. If water made it worse, then what he had done must have been the fix. She set the pitcher down, turned off the burner, and lifted the lid she had left on the table, sliding it over the pan in one steady motion.

The flames died. Under the lid the fire had nothing left, and Anna stood staring at the blackened bacon while her heartbeat slowed. Gwen lowered her phone. "Okay," Gwen said quietly, "that was actually dramatic, and I didn't even get it on camera." She had wanted a flashy clip for the project, but now she wanted something else. "Can we redo the whole thing tomorrow, and this time film the part where you explain it? Because I didn't know any of that."

Anna lifted the lid and checked the pan, which was scorched but not ruined. "You can't put water on a grease fire," she said. "It turns to steam and throws the burning oil everywhere. You turn off the heat and cover it with the lid. That smothers it." Gwen wrote it down on her arm with a pen.

They rinsed the pan and started the bacon again, more carefully this time, and Gwen kept her pitcher of water far away from the burner where it couldn't hinder anything. Anna stirred the rice, tasted it, added soy sauce, and carried the plates toward the back door, where her mother was already waiting with two forks and a grin.

activity: getting a first phone and learning to use it responsibly
knowledge_domain: getting a first phone and learning to use it responsibly
fact: Phone batteries are lithium-ion, and as they chemically age they hold less charge, so battery life slowly gets shorter.
story:
Gavin held the phone in both hands on Dalie's front steps, turning it over like it might have instructions printed on the back. It had belonged to Dalie's older brother, and when Dalie's mom handed it down last week, Gavin had promised his own mother he would prove he could handle it. That was the deal. One month of being responsible, and then it was really his.

By Tuesday of the first week, the phone was dead by lunch. On Wednesday, dead again by lunch. "You're playing games on it all morning," Dalie accused him at the lunch table. "I am not," Gavin said, and he wasn't. He'd only checked the time twice.

Thursday night, sitting cross-legged on Dalie's bedroom floor while Dalie rebuilt a model airplane, Gavin made a list on a napkin. Charged all night. Unplugged at seven. Off by noon. He stared at the numbers and thought about Dalie's brother, who had used this phone for three years, always charging it, always draining it. Emiliano leaned over from the beanbag chair where he was gluing the plane's propeller. "My dad says old phones just do that. The batteries get worn out from being used so long." Gavin looked at the phone. Lithium-ion, it said in tiny print on the box Dalie's brother had left in the closet. The battery wasn't broken. It had just slowly gotten weaker over the years, like a sponge that held less water each time you soaked it.

He tested it. Friday he charged the phone to full, wrote down the percentage every hour, and by fifth period it read eleven percent. Same usage as his friend's new phone, which still showed sixty. That proved it. The battery wasn't his fault.

"It's not my fault," Gavin announced Saturday, back on Dalie's floor, holding up his napkin graph. Dalie frowned. "So you're going to give it back?"

Gavin hadn't thought past proving himself innocent. "No. I'm going to make it work." He ordered a replacement battery online with his allowance, and when it came, Mr. Mensah from next door, who fixed computers in his garage, swapped it in for him in about ten minutes. Sunday night, Gavin charged the phone and wrote 100 percent on a fresh napkin.

Monday at noon the screen still showed seventy percent, and Gavin smiled at it in the cafeteria. Dalie slid into the seat across from him, peering at the screen. "Okay, that's radical," Dalie admitted, then pulled out his own phone, the cracked hand-me-down from his cousin. "Mine dies at two every day. Think you could fix it too?" Gavin looked at the crack, at the old case, at his friend's hopeful face, and put his napkin and his pencil back on the table. "Bring your napkin," he said.

activity: the difference between a scientific claim backed by tested evidence and a story about one person's experience
knowledge_domain: the difference between a scientific claim backed by tested evidence and a story about one person's experience
fact: An anecdote is a story about one person's experience; it cannot show that one thing caused another, because other explanations for what happened have not been ruled out.
story:
Abigail spread her three library books across the table and checked her notebook for the tenth time. Her science fair project was due Friday, and she still didn't have a claim she could actually support. Yousuf slid into the chair across from her and dropped a shiny copper bracelet on top of her notes.

"My uncle sent me this," he said. "He wore one for a month and his back pain went away. He swears by it. I figured you could put it in your project, since your topic is pain or whatever."
