"My topic is evidence," Abigail said. She picked up the bracelet and turned it over. "Yousuf, that's one person's story. It can't show the bracelet caused anything, because other explanations haven't been ruled out."

"Like what?"

"Like maybe his back got better on its own. Maybe he started exercising. Maybe he just wanted it to work." She pulled a worksheet from her folder. "Mr. Do made us sort claims today. A story about one person's experience is called an anecdote. One anecdote isn't evidence, because you haven't ruled anything else out."

Yousuf frowned at the bracelet. "It felt warm when I put it on. That means something."

Abigail glanced toward the front desk, where Mr. Do was checking in a return cart, and an idea landed so hard she almost knocked over her pencil cup. "Wait. We can test it. Not his back, your wrist. You said your wrist aches after gaming."

"So?"

"So we flip a coin. Heads, you wear the real bracelet for a week and write down your pain every night. Tails, you wear this." She dug in her frugal project budget, a slim envelope of allowance money, and counted out coins for the library's lost-and-found bin, where a plain steel ring had sat for months. She'd ask the cashier-priced one at the front, or better, Mr. Do, if she could borrow it. "Same weight, same warmth on skin, no copper."

Yousuf agreed, and they drew a chart with seven boxes each for real and fake. That night he texted her: Wrist pain four out of ten, bracelet on, feels kind of warm. She smiled and logged it.

The week crawled. At school Yousuf reported the pain seemed to diminish by Thursday, which he announced loudly in the cafeteria, and Braydon immediately wanted a copper bracelet too. Abigail kept her face neutral and said nothing, though her stomach tightened every time she thought about Thursday, because of one detail Yousuf didn't know yet. On Monday she had looked up pain studies in the library's medical section and found something that changed everything: in real trials, people wearing fake bracelets reported almost the same improvement as people wearing real ones.

Friday afternoon, they met at the same library table. Yousuf slapped down his completed chart, grinning. "Pain went from four to one. Copper works. I'm telling my uncle he was right."

Abigail slid the chart aside and set the steel ring beside the bracelet. "Flip the coin," she said.

He flipped. Tails.

"You've been wearing the fake all week, Yousuf. No copper at all." She watched his face work through it, the grin collapsing into something between disappointment and wonder. "Your pain got better anyway. So the bracelet can't be what did it, because we didn't rule out it just getting better on its own. That's my whole project. That's the claim with tested evidence behind it."

Yousuf picked up the steel ring and held it next to the copper one, turning them so they caught the window light. Behind them, Mr. Do pushed his cart past the tall shelf, and on the top of it sat a model ship whose cracked hull had been waiting months for repairs.

"Can we run it again next week?" Yousuf asked. "My brother wants in, and he says his knee aches."

Abigail was already drawing a bigger chart. "Tell him to bring his own coin."

activity: recovering from a cold or flu at home
knowledge_domain: recovering from a cold or flu at home
fact: Green or yellow mucus comes from immune cells and an enzyme they release, so its color alone does not show whether an infection is caused by bacteria or a virus.
story:
Katherine sat on her bedroom floor surrounded by crumpled tissues, a box of grape juice, and her phone, which would not stop buzzing. It was Arabella, who had caught the same cold two days before the class trip to the science museum, and Arabella was convinced the trip was doomed.

"LOOK," the message said, with a photo of a tissue that was decidedly green. "My mom says this means bacteria. I need the strong medicine TONIGHT or I can't go Saturday."

Katherine stared at the photo, then at her own wastebasket, where an identical shade of green stared back at her. If Arabella was right, Katherine was doomed too. She pulled her blanket around her shoulders and thought hard. Her dad was at the pharmacy already, picking up her cough syrup. She called him and asked him to do one thing: get the pharmacist talking while she listened on the phone.

"Ask her what the green means," Katherine whispered.

She heard the cashier scanning bandaids in the background, then a woman's voice, patient and quick. "Green or yellow mucus comes from your immune cells, and from an enzyme they release. That's it. The color alone doesn't show whether it's bacteria or a virus. Only a test can sort that out."

Katherine hung up and sat very still, working it through. Her own mucus had turned green on Tuesday, and by Thursday she already felt halfway better. Arabella's had turned green the same day, from the same cold, which everyone knew came from the substitute teacher who sneezed through Monday's math class. A virus, almost certainly. Green didn't mean disaster. Green meant their immune systems were generating whatever that enzyme was, and doing their jobs.

She texted back a short version, then called Arabella for real, because Arabella was pacing her room announcing she'd demand antibiotics at urgent care before it closed at eight. "It's seven fifteen," Arabella said, breathless.

"Listen. Both of us have green. Both of us are improving. Same cold, same sneezing substitute. If green meant bacteria, we'd both need pills, and the pharmacist says it doesn't mean that." Katherine took a sip of juice. "What you need is fluids, sleep, and a flu vaccine in October like Foster's family does, because they never catch anything."

There was a long pause on the line, and then a small, deflated laugh. "So my sophisticated emergency plan was pointless."

"Drink something," Katherine said. "Text me at nine. We'll compare tissues."

activity: to play a piece with dynamics and tempo changes in a band or on the piano
knowledge_domain: to play a piece with dynamics and tempo changes in a band or on the piano
fact: Musical loudness is marked with Italian words: piano means soft and forte means loud.
story:
Nathaniel had been practicing Addyson's piano piece for two weeks, and today was the day he would finally play it with her, both hands, all the way through. Her living room smelled like popcorn, and the big upright piano sat under a window with a brittle little figurine of a dancer on top, so old that one wrong chord might rattle it off the shelf.

"Start at measure twelve," Addyson said, scooting over to make room on the bench. "That's where it gets tricky."

Nathaniel set his hands on the keys and played. When he reached the letter p printed under the notes, he hammered out a huge, glorious sound, because p had to mean powerful, right? He liked that part best. The dancer figurine trembled.

Addyson winced and stopped him. "That's supposed to be the quiet part. Piano means soft and forte means loud. They're Italian words."

Nathaniel stared at the page. So the p was telling him to shrink, not to shout, and the f he'd been playing gently was asking for a whole different animal. He flipped back a page and found a p he'd been blasting for two weeks. "Wait. So every time I thought the music was saying go big, it was actually saying back off?"

"Basically," Addyson said, laughing. "Try it again, but this time imagine you're sneaking downstairs for a midnight snack during the p part."

He tried it. The soft passage came out whispery and careful, and when the f arrived, the loudness actually meant something, because the quiet had made room for it. It was like the piece was breathing. They ran it three more times, and by the third try Nathaniel could feel the pattern in his hands before his eyes confirmed it.

Her little brother wandered in and asked if he could participate, and Addyson let him hold the sustain pedal, which he did with tremendous seriousness, like a tiny employee of a piano corporation who took pedal duty very seriously.

"One more time," Nathaniel said. "All the way through."

They played it, soft where it asked for soft, loud where it asked for loud, her brother pumping the pedal, the dancer figurine swaying on top of the piano but never quite falling. When they hit the final chord, Nathaniel lifted his hands and found they were shaking a little, in a good way.

"Now the fast part," Addyson said, flipping the page. "Tempo change. Ready?"

He set his hands back on the keys.

activity: to test whether a solution is an acid or a base using litmus paper and the pH scale
knowledge_domain: to test whether a solution is an acid or a base using litmus paper and the pH scale
fact: Litmus paper only shows whether a solution is acidic or basic; it cannot tell how strong the acid or base is.
story:
Colton held the tweezers like they were a bomb fuse. "If this turns my lemonade red, I'm drinking nothing but water for the rest of my life," he announced, and Ayoub laughed so hard he nearly knocked over the tray of test samples.

Mr. Ba had set out five unlabelled cups on the lab bench and told them to sort acids from bases with nothing but litmus paper. Neve went first, dipping her blue strip into cup one. It came out pink. "Acid," she said, and wrote it down. Colton retrieved his own strip from the box, tore it in half because he was already running low, and tested cup two. Pink again. Cup three, pink. Cup four turned the paper blue, so that one was a base. But cup five was the strange one, and by the time they got to it, they had three cups that all looked exactly the same shade of discouraged pink.

"They can't all be the same," Colton said, squinting at the three strips laid side by side on a paper towel. The mystery sample, the vinegar, and something Mr. Ba had whispered was drain cleaner, all red, all identical. He dipped a fresh strip into the mystery cup, then into the vinegar, then into the drain cleaner, holding them up to the window light where the smell of vinegar mixed with the sharper chemical sting from cup three. Same pink. Same pink. Same pink.

"That's useless," Ayoub said. "It's like a yes-or-no question that won't tell you how much."

"Litmus only shows whether a solution is acidic or basic," Neve read from the worksheet, tapping the line with her pen. "It cannot tell how strong the acid or base is." Colton stared at the three matching strips, and something clicked, the way a jammed locker door finally gives. "So the drain cleaner could eat a hole in the counter and the vinegar could dress a salad, and this paper treats them like twins. We'd need something else to compare them. A scale or whatever." He said it with the guilt-free confidence of a boy whose conscience was clear, mostly because he had not actually tasted anything.

Mr. Ba drifted over, peered at their three pink strips, and raised one eyebrow. "So what have we learned, gentlemen and Neve?"

"We learned that paper is a terrible gossip," Colton said. "It spills one secret and keeps the rest."

"Then perhaps tomorrow," Mr. Ba said, "I will let you meet the pH scale."

Neve wrote a large question mark next to cup five, underlined it twice, and slid the tray toward the window, where the three identical strips dried to the same stubborn shade of pink.

activity: the way averages, percentages and rankings in sports and news compress many events into one number
knowledge_domain: the way averages, percentages and rankings in sports and news compress many events into one number
fact: A percentage based on very few attempts can be misleading: a player who makes one shot out of one attempt shoots 100 percent.
story:
At dinner, Hailey pushed her noodles around the plate and said, "Veronica claims she has a perfect shooting percentage." Her father looked up from his glass. "Perfect? Nobody's perfect." He said it lightly, but Hailey knew he followed basketball closely enough to argue about it. "She told the whole team she's shooting a hundred percent," Hailey said. "She made one shot in the game against Ridgefield. It was her only shot all season." Her little brother laughed so hard he nearly knocked over his milk.

The problem was real. Coach posted the stats on the gym door every Friday, and Veronica's name sat at the top of the percentage column, above players who had scored dozens of baskets. Some of the seventh graders had started saying Veronica was the best shooter on the team, and Zoha had come home from practice with her jaw tight, saying nothing, which was worse than complaining.

Hailey took her plate to the sink and thought about the numbers while she rinsed it. One shot, one make. Two shots, two makes would be the same percentage. But what about someone who took forty shots and made twenty-five? That was a lower percentage, and yet that player had scored twenty-five baskets for the team, not one. The hot water ran over her hands. She counted on her fingers just to be sure the pattern held, and it did. A percentage built on one single attempt could say "perfect" about a person who had barely played.

The next morning she found Zoha at the lockers before homeroom. "Ask Veronica how many shots she's taken," Hailey said. "Not how many she made. Total." At practice that afternoon, Zoha asked, right in the middle of the gym, with the whole team stretching. Veronica said, "One," and then added, "but I made it, so I'm at one hundred percent." Zoha nodded slowly. "So a player who makes one shot out of one attempt shoots one hundred percent," she said. "Even if she never takes another one."

A few of the seventh graders looked at each other. Veronica looked down at her sneakers. The gym smelled like floor wax and rubber, and the coach's whistle lay silent on the bench. When they ran the shooting drill, Veronica took eleven shots and made four. On Friday the new stats went up on the gym door, and her name had slid down the column. She stood in front of the paper for a long moment, then turned around and said, "Zoha, you take the next practice shots with me. Both of us, ten each."

activity: competing in a spelling bee
knowledge_domain: competing in a spelling bee
fact: In the Scripps National Spelling Bee, a speller may start over, but changing any letters already said counts as a misspelling.
story:
The bleachers in the gymnasium were packed, and Luke could hear his own heartbeat over the squeak of Jordan's sneakers on the sideline. Six spellers were left, and the word hanging in front of him was "millennium."

"M-I-L-E," Luke began, and then the gym went quiet in a way that felt like falling. He heard the wrong letter leave his mouth and knew, instantly, that the right one was E. His mind raced back to the rules sheet Ms. Suryanto had handed out in the library two weeks ago. He had read one line over and over because it had surprised him: you could start a word again from the beginning, but if you changed even one letter you had already said, it counted as a misspelling. Jordan had shrugged when Luke pointed it out. "Who'd ever need that?" Jordan had said. Now Luke knew exactly who.

He could try to slip the correct E in quietly and hope nobody noticed. But Ms. Suryanto was the judge, and she had a habit of leaning forward with her pen stopped mid-air, watching spellers the way she watched kids trying to sneak a second turn at four square. He remembered the spelling bee last year, when a boy had swapped a letter halfway through and Ms. Suryanto had shaken her head before he even finished. Luke had thought it was harsh then. Now he understood it was just obstinate fairness, the kind that never bends.

"May I start over?" Luke asked.

"You may," Ms. Suryanto said, "as long as every letter you say now matches what you said before."

So the letter could not change, only the rest of the word could. He tested the idea in his head, turning it like a puzzle piece. If he said M-I-L-E again, he was stuck with the wrong E where an N belonged, and the word would die right there. Unless the letters he had spoken could belong to a different word entirely. He thought of Henley's trick from their practice sessions, when Henley would ask for the definition to buy time. Luke didn't need time; he needed a redirect.

"M-I-L-E," he repeated, keeping his voice steady, "N-N-I-U-M." He paused. "Milestone. M-I-L-E-S-T-O-N-E. Milestone."

A ripple went through the bleachers. Ms. Suryanto's pen hovered, then her chin dipped, and she said, "Correct." Jordan pumped both fists so hard he grabbed his own knee, and later he would claim he'd bruised the cartilage under the kneecap, which Luke doubted, since Jordan exaggerated everything.

Back at his seat, waiting for the next round, Luke thought about the boy from last year. If he had simply stopped and started over, keeping his letters, he might have survived another round. Maybe the rule wasn't harsh at all; maybe it rewarded the spellers who noticed their own mistakes instead of hiding them. Luke wasn't sure. He decided he'd ask Henley on the walk home.

"Milestone," Henley whispered from the row behind him. "You nurturing that one for weeks?"

"Since the library," Luke whispered back.

Ms. Suryanto cleared her throat and read the next word.

activity: to describe their family and pets in a new language using full sentences
knowledge_domain: to describe their family and pets in a new language using full sentences
fact: Mandarin Chinese puts a measure word between a number and a noun: "one cat" is "yì zhī māo," where "zhī" is the measure word used for many animals.
story:
Zoe had recruited Blaine to quiz her before the Mandarin quiz on Friday, mostly because Blaine was the only person she knew who would actually say "no" when she got something wrong. They sat on the bleachers behind the gym, and Blaine held her notebook like a judge holding a verdict.

"Describe your family," Blaine read. "Full sentences."

"Wǒ yǒu yī gè mèimei," Zoe said. "I have one little sister."

"Good. Pets."

"Wǒ yǒu yī māo."

Blaine squinted at the notebook. "There's supposed to be a little word in there. It says so."

"That can't be right," Zoe said. "It's not in the sentence about my sister."

She tested it anyway, because testing things was faster than arguing with Blaine. She said the sentence both ways, over and over, into her phone's recorder, and played them back. The short one sounded like she was dropping something halfway through, like a stair with a missing step. That night she wrote to her grandmother, who lived two towns over and video-called every Sunday.

Dear Pópo, she wrote. How do I say "I have one cat"? I keep saying it wrong and I don't know which part is missing.

The reply came Thursday, in her grandmother's careful handwriting, scanned and emailed by an aunt. The cat says māo, the letter began, as if Zoe didn't know that. The number goes first, then a small word, then the cat. One cat is yì zhī māo. The small word, zhī, is the one we use for many animals. You would not say the number and then the cat with nothing between them, any more than you would wear an elastic band without stretching it around something. Your sister, by the way, uses a different small word. Ask your teacher.

Zoe read the letter three times. So that was the pattern. Numbers and animals needed something in the middle, and it wasn't the same something for every noun. She made two columns in her notebook, one for sister words and one for cat words, and practiced until her pen ran dry.

Friday, Mr. Robinson walked the rows listening to each student. When he reached Zoe, she pulled off the elastic holding her hair back, because she somehow spoke better with her hands free.

"Wǒ yǒu yì zhī māo," she said. "And she is enormous."

"Duì," said Mr. Robinson, and moved on.

Blaine raised a hand. "Settlement of a bet," he announced. "Zoe owes me a cookie. She said the little word didn't matter."

"Cookie," Zoe said, and slid one across the desk.

activity: to do a load of laundry from sorting colours to folding
knowledge_domain: to do a load of laundry from sorting colours to folding
fact: Laundry is sorted by colour because new dark or bright clothes can release dye into the wash water, and that dye can tint white and pale clothes.
story:
Payton dragged the laundry basket into the garage and tipped it onto the overturned canoe that leaned against the wall, using the smooth hull as a sorting table. Her mom had left a note on the dryer three days ago: "Learn this. White shirt must be clean by Friday." Friday was tomorrow, and Payton had exactly one load's worth of time.

"Sorting is a waste," she said when Zane and Kaiya biked over and found her staring at the pile. "It's all getting washed in the same machine anyway." Zane shrugged and sat on an upturned bucket while Payton stuffed everything, dark jeans, her new red socks, dish towels, and the white school shirt, into the washer and slammed the lid. Kaiya squinted at the machine like it was a bear trap. "My gran sorts by colour," she offered. "My mom doesn't," Payton said, "and her clothes look fine." The drum rumbled, water beginning to circulate through the window in the lid, swirling soap and clothes into a grey-blue storm.

When the cycle ended, Payton pulled out the white shirt and held it up. It was pale pink. Not uniformly pink, which might have been almost stylish, but blotchy, like a sunset that had given up halfway. Zane laughed so hard he slid off the bucket. "Nice shirt. Very expensive-looking."

Payton laid the pink shirt on the canoe hull and picked up one of the red socks. She thought about the order of events. The shirt had been white when it went in. It came out pink. Nothing else had touched it except water, soap, and clothes, and the only red thing in the load was this brand-new sock. Her gran's new towels had felt damp with dye when she'd hugged them at the store. Maybe, she thought, new dark or bright clothes could let dye go into the wash water, and that dye could tint white and pale clothes. She could test it. She filled a jar with warm water, dropped in the red sock, and set the jar on the workbench where they could all watch.

Within minutes, wisps of red curled off the sock like smoke. "It's bleeding," Kaiya whispered. "So that's the whole point of sorting," Payton said slowly. She had changed her mind completely, and she said so. They found one more clean white thing, an old pillowcase, and laid it flat on the hull. "Neutrals and pale stuff in this pile," Payton said, pointing, "dark and bright in that one. New red sock gets its own jar until it stops bleeding." She reloaded the washer with only the dark load, then held up the pink shirt and studied it, chewing her lip. "Tomorrow," she said, "we find out if pink counts as a school colour."

activity: tone differences, public versus private spaces and common conventions of online communication
knowledge_domain: tone differences, public versus private spaces and common conventions of online communication
fact: Psychologist John Suler described the 'online disinhibition effect' in 2004: people often say things online that they would hold back from saying face to face.
story:
The comment appeared on the class discussion board at 10:14 a.m., while twenty keyboards clattered in the computer lab. "Nobody wants your stupid robot pictures, Eliana. Delete them." Alex read it twice. The username was RobotKing77, which told him nothing, because everyone in Ms. Sadeghi's fifth period hid behind usernames.

Eliana sat two rows over, staring at her screen, not typing anymore. That was the strange part. Whoever RobotKing77 was, he had watched Eliana post her robot artwork all week, and he had waited until today to strike. Alex thought about Alvin, who sat behind Eliana in every class and told her, just yesterday, that her drawings belonged in a museum. Alvin was so polite in person that he apologized to chairs when he bumped into them. But usernames were like masks, and masks made some people brave.

Alex remembered something from October, a memory that now felt important. He had been at his grandmother's house, and his cousin had typed something snarky about a referee on a fan forum, something the cousin would never yell at an actual game. "It's just the internet," the cousin had said, laughing. At the time Alex had laughed too. Now he wondered if there was a pattern here, some rule he couldn't see.

He opened a search window and typed slowly, evaluating each result before he clicked. A psychology article came up, and he leaned close to read it under his breath. "In 2004, a psychologist named John Suler described the online disinhibition effect. People often say things online that they would hold back from saying face to face." He read it again. The words fit Alvin perfectly, but they also fit half the class. He needed proof, not a theory.

So he tested it. He posted, as himself, "RobotKing77, Eliana's robot art is the best thing on this board. Show us yours." Public. Signed. Impossible to hide behind. Then he watched the room instead of the screen, because a comment doesn't write itself; somebody's hands have to do it. Three keyboards went quiet. Somebody coughed. Alvin's hands stayed frozen above the keys, and his ears turned a distinct shade of pink that Alex could see even from across the lab.

The reply came at 10:31. "Sorry Eliana. That was dumb. Your robots are cool." No username attached. The next morning, Alvin left a folded drawing on Eliana's desk, a robot with a tiny crown. Eliana unfolded it, looked at Alvin, and said, "RobotKing, I presume?" Alvin's whole face went red, and she held out her hand and said, "Truce?"

activity: customs such as greetings, gift-giving and table manners that differ between cultures and households
knowledge_domain: customs such as greetings, gift-giving and table manners that differ between cultures and households
fact: In Japan, bowing is a common greeting, and generally the longer and deeper the bow, the more respect it shows.
story:
Addison stood outside the Sakura Restaurant holding a wrapped box of maple candies so tightly the ribbon dug into her thumb. Nadia's grandparents had just arrived from Osaka, and Nadia had invited her to dinner, and now Addison had one enormous problem: she had no idea how to greet them. Nadia had drilled her on some things at school, like taking off shoes and not sticking chopsticks upright in rice, but the bowing part was a mystery.

Through the window she watched the door open. Nadia's grandfather bowed to Mr. Mokoena, the owner, and Mr. Mokoena bowed back, and then Nadia's grandmother bowed to a waitress, and the waitress bowed, and everyone in the whole restaurant seemed to be folding at each other like grass in the wind. Addison noticed something. When the grandfather greeted Mr. Mokoena, his bow was quick and shallow, but when Nadia's grandmother met an elderly man by the counter, both of them bent low and held it for a long moment, almost long enough for Addison to have counted to three. A pattern, she thought. Maybe the deeper and longer the bow, the more respect it showed. That was testable.

"Addison! You're early," Nadia said, pulling her inside.

"I have a theory," Addison whispered. "Bowing is like a respect meter. Deep and long means big respect."

"Shh. They're coming. Say konnichiwa. You can do this. I nominate you for bravest friend in the cafeteria."

The grandparents approached. Addison handed over the candy box with both hands, because Nadia had said gifts were given that way and were often refused once or twice before being accepted. Grandmother said, "Oh, you must not," and Addison held on politely, and after the second refusal, exactly as predicted, the gift was accepted with a small bow. Addison bent down low and slow, the way she'd seen done for the elderly man. When she peeked upward, grandfather was smiling, and grandmother bowed back even deeper, so deep that Addison, who had just learned the word in geometry, thought her spine was nearly perpendicular to the floor.

At the table, things got trickier. Addison lifted her bowl of rice to her mouth the way Nadia did, and slurped her noodles, which felt absolutely wrong after years of being told to be quiet at dinner, but grandmother nodded approval and slurped louder, so Addison slurped louder too, and Nadia laughed so hard she nearly dropped her chopsticks.

"So," Nadia said as they waited for tea. "Grandmother says you bowed better than our mail carrier. He waves. Just waves, like he's landing a plane."

"He doesn't know the system," Addison said. "The system is deep bow, big respect."

"Exactly. You figured it out in one minute through a window."

Grandfather leaned over and, in careful English, said, "Your bow was very kind. Next time, maybe not so deep. You are young. You save your knees."

Addison grinned and bowed, quick and shallow, just enough. Grandfather bowed back the same way.

activity: to prepare for a coming-of-age ceremony by learning a reading or prayer by heart
knowledge_domain: to prepare for a coming-of-age ceremony by learning a reading or prayer by heart
fact: A Torah reader follows the words with a yad, a pointer whose name means hand, so that the parchment itself is not touched.
story:
Jasmine stood in her grandmother's kitchen with a photocopied page of Torah verses, and around her the whole family was pretending not to listen while absolutely listening. Her aunt stirred a pot very slowly. Her grandfather set down his teacup with exaggerated care, as if a loud clink might ruin everything.

"Again," said Ms. Ross, the neighbour who had been tutoring her since September. She had come to the gathering on purpose, carrying a cloth bag, because the bat mitzvah was in nine days and Jasmine's confidence kept dwindling every time she stumbled on the same phrase in verse twelve.

Jasmine took a breath and began. She got through verse four, verse seven, even the tricky part she'd nicknamed "the tongue twister." Then her grandmother brought out the real thing, a small Torah scroll borrowed from the synagogue for the occasion, and unrolled it on the table. Jasmine's hands went cold. Somehow reading off parchment was nothing like reading off a photocopy. Her voice shrank, and before she knew it her finger drifted toward the letters, hovering closer and closer, until Ms. Ross gently placed something in her other hand.

It was a slim silver pointer, shaped like a tiny hand at the end. "It's called a yad," Ms. Ross said, and nothing more.

"Yad means hand," Jasmine said slowly, turning it over. "That's why it's shaped like this." Nobody answered, which was how she knew she'd gotten it right. She followed the words with the pointer instead of her finger, and realized something: the reason she'd been stumbling wasn't nerves at all. When her finger hovered over the letters, she was blocking her own view of the line, then losing her place when she moved it. The pointer sat just above the words and traveled with her, steady as a bookmark that walked.

She remembered Brent, her lab partner, laughing about his science fair prototype, a volcano that had gone extinct halfway through the demonstration. "At least it fizzled in front of the class instead of the judges," he'd said. "Practice where you fail." So she practiced right there, in front of twelve relatives and a pot of soup.

Verse by verse, with the yad in her hand, the reading came out clean. When she finished, her grandfather raised his teacup like a toast.

Her little cousin tugged her sleeve. "Can I hold the hand stick?"

"After the ceremony," Jasmine said, "I'll teach you the tongue twister."

activity: saying goodbye to a grandparent who has died
knowledge_domain: saying goodbye to a grandparent who has died
fact: In their 1999 dual process model, researchers Margaret Stroebe and Henk Schut described grieving people as moving back and forth between focusing on the loss and getting on with daily life.
story:
Wyatt sat in the third pew of the synagogue with his father's suit jacket buttoned to the top, because Grandma Ruth had always said a boy should look like he cared. At the front, next to the rabbi, stood a small table with her glasses folded on it. Freya slid into the pew beside him and whispered, "My mom said to tell you we're sorry. Also, Leia is parking the bike, so save her a spot." Wyatt saved the spot. He had a plan for the service, which he had written on an index card in his desk the night before: say the mourner's prayer, look at the glasses, remember her voice, feel something. He had tested the plan twice in rehearsal and both times it had worked, more or less.

The week before, he had gone with Leia to a movie because she had won two tickets and had been talking about it for a month. He had laughed hard at the talking dog, and then, walking out into the arid July parking lot, he had felt like he had betrayed someone. He came home and told his father, "I laughed the same week she died. That's wrong." His father didn't lecture him. He only pulled a paperback off the shelf, one with a cracked spine, and said, "Chapter four. Read it yourself, then evaluate whether you're a bad grandson."

The book was by two researchers, Margaret Stroebe and Henk Schut. In 1999, they had described grieving people as moving back and forth between focusing on the loss and getting on with daily life. They called it the dual process model. Wyatt had read the page three times, checking his premise against the evidence: Grandma died on a Tuesday, and he had still eaten breakfast on Wednesday, still done his homework, still laughed at Leia's impressions in the cafeteria. According to the model, that was not betrayal. That was the back-and-forth, the ordinary rhythm of it, loss then life then loss again.

Freya had her own reason for being there. She was collecting signatures on a memory card for Wyatt's family, and she wanted everyone at the shiva afterward to sign it too, which meant she kept slipping out to the lobby with a pen. When she came back the fourth time, Mr. Szabó, who taught science at their school and had known Grandma from the community garden, leaned over the pew. "I heard your father mention the dual process model," he said quietly. "It's why I'm crying and then telling jokes in the same ten minutes."

Leia arrived just as the congregation stood for the prayer. Wyatt's voice shook, steadied, and shook again. Afterward he walked to the small table, picked up her glasses, folded his hand around them, and said, "Thanks for the dog movie, Grandma. You'd have hated it."

activity: to ask for directions in a new language and understand the answer
knowledge_domain: to ask for directions in a new language and understand the answer
fact: In Spanish, the question "¿Dónde está...?" means "Where is...?", and adding "por favor" makes it polite.
story:
The festival crowd in Sevilla was so thick that Luke lost Riley within thirty seconds of stepping through the gate. Worse, he lost the meeting spot too, because the meeting spot had been a giant paper lantern shaped like a bull, and the wind had just knocked it down. His phone was dead, his mom was somewhere near the flamenco stage, and his stomach was doing that desperate thing it did when he had drunk two lemonades at lunch and then walked for an hour.

He had one phrase ready. Ms. Littlechild, his Spanish teacher back home, had drilled it into the whole class before the trip, standing at the whiteboard while the clock ticked toward the bell. "If you remember nothing else," she had said, tapping the marker, "remember this one." Luke had written it on his hand that morning in the hotel, and the ink was still faintly there under the sunscreen: ¿Dónde está el baño? He also remembered Riley grinning beside him, whispering that the blue wristbands Ms. Littlechild handed out symbolized survival, since without them none of them would make it home.

The problem was the answer. He knew how to ask, but when a woman by the paella stand replied in a rapid stream of Spanish, he caught only one word, and it was not a direction. "Le... izquierda?" he guessed, and she laughed kindly and repeated herself, slower this time, pointing with two fingers as if turning a tiny steering wheel. Left. The word must mean left. He said "por favor," the way Riley had practiced with him on the plane, and the woman's whole face softened, and she walked him three steps to a corner and pointed again.

Luke thanked her with the only other word he had, "gracias," and jogged left, where a green sign with a stick figure waited behind a row of flags that symbolized every country represented at the festival. The relief was immediate and enormous. On the way out he spotted Riley by a churro cart, holding two churros like a diplomat holding important documents, his face serious. "I've been negotiating," Riley said. "This nice man only speaks Spanish, and I've been saying 'por favor' at him for ten minutes. I think it means he has to be nice to me now."

"It makes it polite," Luke said, mouth already full of churro. "It's like magic manners." Riley stared at him, then turned back to the churro man and said "por favor" one more time, very slowly, and the man laughed and handed over a third churro, free. Behind them, a loudspeaker announced that the lantern parade, the one mandatory event their whole group had traveled to see, would begin in five minutes. Luke grabbed Riley's sleeve and pointed down the boulevard, where the first paper lanterns were already being lit. "Left is that way. Trust me, I speak Spanish now."

activity: persuasion techniques such as bandwagon appeals, loaded words and celebrity testimonials used in ads and propaganda
knowledge_domain: persuasion techniques such as bandwagon appeals, loaded words and celebrity testimonials used in ads and propaganda
fact: The word "propaganda" comes from a Catholic Church committee for spreading the faith, the Congregatio de Propaganda Fide, set up by Pope Gregory XV in 1622.
story:
Gavin had forty dollars, and the sneakers in the window of the mall's sportswear store cost one hundred and thirty. He stood there with his vocabulary worksheet crumpled in his back pocket, doing the math twice in case the first answer was a mistake. It wasn't. The shoes glowed under the spotlights like they were radioactive.

"Everybody's wearing them," said Jaxon, who had appeared beside him out of nowhere, holding a smoothie. "The whole eighth grade. Jet has two pairs."

Jet, as it happened, was inside the store, holding up a box and grinning. Gavin went in. The walls were covered with a poster of a basketball player he recognized from TV, mid-dunk, wearing the exact shoe. Underneath, the words read: LIMITED. FEARLESS. REVOLUTIONARY. Elite players demand more. Gavin read it twice. The words felt like they were shouting at him, even though they were printed on paper.

He took out the worksheet, which was for Mr. Anderson's class and due Monday. The assignment was to look up the history of one vocabulary word, and Gavin had picked "propaganda" because it had sounded dramatic. He'd found the entry that morning and it had surprised him so much he'd read it out loud to his mom. "The word propaganda comes from a Catholic Church committee for spreading the faith, the Congregatio de Propaganda Fide, set up by Pope Gregory XV in 1622," he told Jaxon, who sipped his smoothie and said, "Huh. I thought it just meant lying."

"It kind of started as spreading an idea on purpose," Gavin said, looking around the store. "Like this." He pointed at the poster. "That's a celebrity testimonial. Jet having two pairs is a bandwagon appeal. And 'fearless' is a loaded word, because shoes can't actually be brave." He felt like a detective who had just exposed a whole criminal operation, except the criminals were posters and the crime was making him want shoes he couldn't afford.

Jet came over, box in hand. "You getting them?"

"I have forty bucks."

"They'd change your whole life," Jet said, and Gavin noticed Jet said it in the exact tone of the TV commercial, which made him laugh until his stomach hurt, somewhere up near his intestine, which he was pretty sure wasn't where stomachaches actually happened but close enough.

The clerk announced over the speaker that the shoes were selling out fast and restocking was not guaranteed. Two kids behind them shifted impatiently. It all felt suddenly inevitable, like a machine designed to end with Gavin's forty dollars in the register.

He tested his idea instead. He turned to the clearance rack, where last year's model sat, nearly identical, for thirty-five dollars. He tried them on. They fit. He carried the box to the register, paid, and walked out with five dollars left for a pretzel.

Jaxon caught up to him by the fountain. "You know those are basically the same shoe."

Gavin held up the box. "Fearless," he said, "and on clearance."
